**Audience**: an engineer who already runs Adam or SGD and wants to know *why* it converges (or not). **Empirical first**: each topic starts from a symptom — a loss that oscillates because the step is too large, a plateau on an ill-conditioned problem — and only then names the concepts that explain it: convexity, conditioning, acceleration, proximal operators, convergence rates.

The module is the theoretical backbone reused wherever a model is trained in the program.

### What you will be able to do

-   Prove the convergence of gradient descent and its acceleration under convexity and strong convexity assumptions.
-   Explain the role of conditioning and that of Nesterov acceleration.
-   Handle non-smooth objectives with proximal methods (ISTA, FISTA).
-   Analyze stochastic gradient descent and the effect of variance reduction (SAGA, SVRG).
-   Choose between first-order and quasi-Newton methods according to the problem and its dimension.
-   Formulate constraints in learning via duality, projections and penalties.
-   Optimize hyperparameters in a reasoned way rather than blindly.
-   Connect these theoretical results to the actual training of neural networks.

### Official objectives and syllabus (2026-2027 catalog)

According to the [APM_52067_EP — “Optimization for AI”](https://synapses.polytechnique.fr/catalogue/2026-2027/ue/23796/APM-52067-EP-optimization-for-ai) sheet: the course introduces the fundamentals of optimization for machine learning and AI. Rather than a panorama of existing algorithms, it is organized around the workhorse of modern ML/AI — stochastic gradient descent (SGD) — and studies its extensions, such as variance reduction and adaptive methods, deriving convergence guarantees in convex and non-convex settings.

It also explores minimax optimization, in particular in the context of constrained optimization and duality, non-smooth optimization, and saddle-point methods, with an emphasis on theoretical foundations and practical applications.

The sheet publishes no session-by-session programme and no prerequisites. The LLGA section of its assessment tab gives only the exam format: a written final exam without calculator, with one handwritten A4 sheet allowed (to be handed in with the exam). ### Where this course fits in the program

An option of period 2 of M1, outside the recommended track. It sits in the Choose-1 group of Period 2, next to Multimodal Generative AI, [Deep Learning (P2 variant)](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html), [Computational Optimal Transport](../m1p2-optimal-transport/index.html), Advanced Deep Learning and Image Synthesis. A student who takes it takes none of these, so this page cites their notes only as optional reading. Official prerequisites: not communicated (the “Prerequisites” tab of the SynapseS sheet is empty).

What the module assumes:

-   the mandatory P1 [Machine Learning](../m1p1-machine-learning/index.html) course, whose gradient descent (0.2) and Lagrangian duality (0.4) are recalled in chapter 0;
-   the P1 [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html) course, which every student of this option has taken: Deep Learning is required once, and its P2 variant sits in this same group. Its Adam and schedules (3.3–3.4) are recalled in chapter 10;
-   if you took it in P1, [Emerging Subjects in ML & Collaborative Learning](../m1p1-emerging-ml/index.html) (SGD review in ch. 0, distributed SGD in ch. 2) is a first draft of chapters 5–6; it is not required.

What it feeds: the mandatory [Reinforcement Learning](../m1p2-reinforcement-learning/index.html) course, which runs in parallel, rests on the stochastic approximation of its section 0.2, and chapter 11 here carries duality over to constrained reinforcement learning. In Year 2, the training runs of [Large Language Models](../m2-large-language-models/index.html) (ch. 3–4) are the SGD, AdamW and schedules of chapters 5 and 10. The [end-of-year projects](../../projects/index.html) Y1.3 (exposure constraint by stochastic primal–dual) and Y2.4 use the constraint tools of chapter 8.

### Course outline

-   **Refresher: convexity and duality** — the essentials of convex analysis reloaded for the rest of the module.
-   **Optimization inside the AI loop** — why modern learning is first an optimization problem, and what that imposes.
-   **Gradient descent: convergence proved** — the founding theorem, its assumptions and its rate, proved in detail.
-   **Conditioning and Nesterov acceleration** — what the geometry of the problem does to speed, and the acceleration that answers it.
-   **Proximal methods: ISTA and FISTA** — handling non-differentiabilities (regularizations, constraints) cleanly, and the subgradient method when no prox is available.
-   **Stochastic gradient descent** — the workhorse algorithm of machine learning, analyzed as such, in the convex and the non-convex settings.
-   **Variance reduction: SAGA and SVRG** — keeping the best of both worlds: the cost of the stochastic, the accuracy of the deterministic.
-   **Newton and quasi-Newton** — exploiting curvature, and doing so at a controlled cost.
-   **Constraints in machine learning** — duality, projections and penalties to encode what the model must respect, and the minimax and saddle-point methods that solve the resulting games.
-   **Hyperparameter optimization** — optimizing the level above: methods, costs and pitfalls.
-   **Optimizing the training of networks** — the junction with practice: adaptive methods (AdaGrad, Adam) and what theory really illuminates in heavy training runs.
-   **Course research notes — CMAP (Chamon, Dieuleveut)** — the instructors' papers, read with the module's tools.
-   **Exercises** — proofs and implementations for each family of algorithms.
-   **Projects and assessment** — solo and group project subjects, a written-exam proposal and a grading rubric.
-   **References** — the theoretical sources of each chapter.

### How to study this module

-   Redo every proof on the board, without the notes: convergence rates are the heart of the exam as of the module.
-   Never separate an algorithm from its assumptions: convexity, L-Lipschitz continuity and strong convexity change everything.
-   Implement each method on simple problems where the exact solution is known, and check the observed rates against the proven rates.
-   Keep chapter 0 at hand: convexity and duality return at every turn.
-   Connect every result to the P1 machine learning module: regularization, SVM and regression become concrete examples.
-   Prepare the exercises in a small group, but write the proofs alone: it is the writing that reveals the gaps.

::: note
[Independent note]{.tag} Optimization is the common grammar of AI: it connects the M2 LLMs (whose training is a vast optimization task) to distributed systems and frugal AI. The theoretical perspective gained here — knowing what an algorithm can and cannot do — distinguishes the engineer who designs from the one who configures, and is a natural prerequisite toward careers in research and large-scale ML.
:::

### Notation {#notation}

The page follows the site-wide [notation conventions](../../notation/index.html):

-   the step (learning rate) is $\eta$ in every chapter, deterministic or stochastic;
-   a momentum coefficient is $\beta$, and Nesterov's is $\beta_k$;
-   $L$ is a smoothness constant, $\mu$ a strong-convexity constant and $\kappa = L/\mu$;
-   a loss is written $\ell(\hat y, y)$, prediction first.

**Deviations, as in optimization textbooks.**

-   From chapter 2 on, the variable of an algorithm is written $x$: it is the parameter $\theta$ of definition 1.1, never a data point. In chapters 5–6, data enter only through the per-sample losses $f_i$, with $f = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i f_i$.
-   Where chapter 8 writes a learning problem with its data (definition 8.1, adversarial training, the SVM of example 8.5), the parameter is again $\theta$ (or $w$) and $x_i$ is an input.
-   In the FISTA proof (chapter 4), $t_k$ is the momentum sequence of Beck and Teboulle, not a step.
-   With a sample index, $y_i$ is the label of sample $i$. Otherwise $y$ is an auxiliary vector: a comparison point in proofs, the look-ahead point $y_k$ of Nesterov and FISTA (chapters 3–4), the gradient difference of BFGS (chapter 7), or the maximizing player of a game (chapter 8).
-   The Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}(x, \lambda)$ is minimized in $x$ and maximized in $\lambda$.

## 0. Refresher: convexity and duality {#ch0}

:::: recap
::: recap-title
L3 reminders — the essentials of convex analysis, complete here (first met in Machine Learning, sections 0.2 and 0.4)
:::

-   **Convexity**: $f\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ is convex if
    $$
    f(\lambda x + (1-\lambda)y) \leq \lambda f(x) + (1-\lambda) f(y) \quad \text{for all } \lambda \in [0,1];
    $$
    in finite dimension with $f$ differentiable, this is equivalent to
    $$
    f(y) \geq f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x), y - x \rangle \quad \text{(subgradient inequality).}
    $$
-   **Strong convexity**: $x \mapsto f(x) - \tfrac{\mu}{2}\|x\|^2$ is convex for some $\mu > 0$ — the subgradient inequality becomes strict by a quadratic term; this is what will yield *linear* (geometric) convergence.
-   **Smoothness**: $\nabla f$ $L$-Lipschitz — that is, $\|\nabla f(x) - \nabla f(y)\| \leq L \|x - y\|$; equivalent to the quadratic upper bound
    $$
    f(y) \leq f(x) + \langle \nabla f(x), y-x\rangle + \tfrac{L}{2}\|y-x\|^2.
    $$
-   **Lagrangian duality**: primal problem $\min f(x)$ subject to $g_i(x) \leq 0$ for $i = 1, \dots, m$, Lagrangian
    $$
    \mathcal{L}(x, \lambda) = f(x) + \sum_i \lambda_i g_i(x),
    $$
    dual function $d(\lambda) = \inf_x \mathcal{L}(x,\lambda)$, dual problem $\max_{\lambda \geq 0} d(\lambda)$.
-   **KKT conditions** (convex differentiable $f$ and $g_i$): $x^\star$ and $\lambda^\star$ solve the primal and the dual with a zero gap if and only if
    $$
    g_i(x^\star) \leq 0, \qquad \lambda^\star \geq 0, \qquad \nabla f(x^\star) + \sum_i \lambda_i^\star \nabla g_i(x^\star) = 0, \qquad \lambda_i^\star\, g_i(x^\star) = 0 \;\; \forall i,
    $$
    that is primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity of the Lagrangian in $x$, and complementary slackness (an inactive constraint has a zero multiplier).
-   **Linear programs**: for $\min c^\top x$ subject to $Ax \geq b$, the dual function is $b^\top \lambda$ when $A^\top\lambda = c$ and $-\infty$ otherwise, so the dual is again a linear program:
    $$
    \max_{\lambda \geq 0}\; b^\top \lambda \quad \text{subject to} \quad A^\top \lambda = c .
    $$
::::

:::: prop
[Proposition 0.1 — Weak duality (proved)]{.tag} For every feasible $x$ and every $\lambda \geq 0$: $d(\lambda) \leq f(x)$. In particular
$$
\max_\lambda d(\lambda) \leq \min_{x \text{ feasible}} f(x) :
$$
the dual always provides lower bounds.

::: proof
For feasible $x$, $g_i(x) \leq 0$ and $\lambda_i \geq 0$ give
$$
\mathcal{L}(x, \lambda) = f(x) + \sum_i \lambda_i g_i(x) \leq f(x).
$$
Taking the infimum over $x$ on the left and then the supremum over $\lambda$, we get $d(\lambda) \leq f(x)$ for every pair, hence
$$
\sup_\lambda d(\lambda) \leq \inf_{x \text{ feasible}} f(x).
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 0.2 — Strong duality (Slater)]{.tag} If the problem is convex (functions $f, g_i$ convex) and there exists a *strictly* feasible point ($g_i(x_0) < 0$ for every $i$; affine constraints only need $g_i(x_0) \leq 0$), then the optimal dual value equals the primal value and the maximum of the dual problem is attained. The **duality gap** (the difference between the two) is zero: this is the key that allows, in chapter 8, replacing a constrained problem with a sequence of unconstrained problems playing on $\lambda$.
:::

::: note
[Why this refresher opens the module]{.tag} All of supervised learning is an optimization problem: minimize an empirical risk $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \ell(f_\theta(x_i), y_i)$ over $\theta$. The three structures of the refresher — convexity, smoothness, duality — determine the choice of algorithm (chapters 2–8) and its speed. Duality will return twice: for constraints (ch. 8, and L. Chamon's work on learning under constraints, ch. 11) and to understand what "learning" means when one imposes requirements (fairness, safety) rather than a mere average cost.
:::

## 1. Optimization inside the AI loop {#ch1}

A fine-tuning run that "stops descending" while the gradient is not zero is usually a problem of conditioning, not a bug. Before any algorithm, this chapter writes training as an optimization problem, fixes the vocabulary, and collects the examples on which every later method is tested.

::: note
[What breaks]{.tag} Three mistakes recur in practice: ignoring the conditioning of the problem, reading a convergence rate proved in expectation as a promise about one run, and differentiating a non-smooth regularizer instead of handling it with a proximal step (ch. 4).
:::

The practitioner's main enemy is *conditioning*; the main ally is *structure* (convexity, separability, sparsity).

::: def
[Definition 1.1 — Training problem]{.tag} Given data $(x_i, y_i)_{i \leq n}$, a parametric model $h_\theta$ and a loss $\ell$, training solves
$$
\min_{\theta \in \mathbb{R}^d}\; F(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(h_\theta(x_i), y_i) \;+\; \Omega(\theta),
$$
where $\Omega$ (penalty) encodes a prior — sparsity $\Omega = \lambda\|\theta\|_1$, stability $\Omega = \tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|_2^2$.

Let $f$ denote the differentiable part (the empirical risk) and $g = \Omega$ the possibly non-differentiable part: this decomposition $F = f + g$ structures chapters 4 and 8.
:::

| Problem | $f(\theta)$ | $g$ | Structure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Least squares | $\frac{1}{2n}\|X\theta - y\|^2$ | — | $\mu$-strongly convex if $\mathrm{rank}(X)=d$, $L$-smooth |
| LASSO | $\frac{1}{2n}\|X\theta - y\|^2$ | $\lambda\|\theta\|_1$ | convex, non-differentiable at 0 (ch. 4) |
| Logistic regression | $\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \log(1+e^{-y_i \theta^\top x_i})$ | 0 or $\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2$ | smooth convex; finite sum (ch. 5–6) |
| SVM (constrained form) | $\tfrac{1}{2}\|\theta\|^2$ | constraints $1 - y_i\theta^\top x_i \leq 0$ | constraints: duality (ch. 8, see ML module ch. 3) |
| Neural network | cross-entropy over $h_\theta$ | — | non-convex (ch. 10) |

::: def
[Definition 1.2 — Subdifferential, reference examples]{.tag} The subdifferential of a convex $F$ at $\theta$ is the set of slopes of the affine minorants that touch $F$ at $\theta$:
$$
\partial F(\theta) = \{v : F(\theta') \geq F(\theta) + \langle v, \theta'-\theta\rangle \;\forall \theta'\}.
$$
It reduces to the singleton $\{\nabla F(\theta)\}$ when $F$ is differentiable at $\theta$. Examples:

-   for $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, $\partial |\theta| = \{\mathrm{sign}(\theta)\}$ if $\theta \neq 0$, $=[-1,1]$ if $\theta = 0$;
-   $\partial (\tfrac{1}{2}\|\theta\|^2) = \{\theta\}$;
-   $\partial \max(\theta_1,\theta_2) = \{e_{i^\star}\}$ if a unique argmax, a segment otherwise.

Summation rule: if one of the two terms is continuous, $\partial(F_1+F_2) = \partial F_1 + \partial F_2$.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 1.3 — First-order optimality condition]{.tag} Let $F$ be convex. Then $\theta^\star$ minimizes $F$ if and only if
$$
0 \in \partial F(\theta^\star).
$$

::: proof
Both directions read definition 1.2 with $v = 0$: the statement $0 \in \partial F(\theta^\star)$ means
$$
F(\theta) \geq F(\theta^\star) + \langle 0, \theta - \theta^\star\rangle = F(\theta^\star) \quad \text{for every } \theta,
$$
which is exactly the statement that $\theta^\star$ minimizes $F$. [∎]{.qed}
:::

The condition does not say that the subdifferential is $\{0\}$: for $F(\theta) = |\theta|$, the minimizer $0$ has $\partial F(0) = [-1, 1]$, which contains $0$. Example 1.4 uses exactly this freedom.
::::

:::: ex
[Example 1.4 — One-dimensional LASSO, by hand]{.tag} Minimize $\frac{1}{2}(z - \theta)^2 + \lambda|\theta|$ over $\theta \in \mathbb{R}$, with $z \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\lambda > 0$. Optimality conditions:

-   either $\theta \neq 0$ and $\theta - z + \lambda\,\mathrm{sign}(\theta) = 0$, hence $\theta = z - \lambda\mathrm{sign}(\theta)$;
-   or $\theta = 0$ and $-z \in [-\lambda, \lambda]$.

We recover **soft thresholding**

::: key
[Key result — soft thresholding]{.tag}
$$
\theta^\star = \mathrm{sign}(z)\,\max(|z|-\lambda,\,0) = S_\lambda(z),
$$
:::

the central operation of chapter 4: sparsity comes from the fact that the optimum "sticks" to zero for all $|z| \leq \lambda$ — which the $\ell_2$ penalty never does.
::::

::: note
[What the module proves, and why]{.tag} At the end of the module, the student must be able to **prove**: the $O(1/k)$ convergence of gradient descent (ch. 2), its linear convergence under strong convexity (ch. 2), the rates of ISTA and FISTA (ch. 4), the stationary regime of constant-step SGD (ch. 5) and the local quadratic convergence of Newton (ch. 7).

The lower bound that makes the $\sqrt{\kappa}$ factor of acceleration optimal (ch. 3) is to be **stated and explained**; its proof is left to the references. Each proof fits in a few lines of well-chosen inequalities — that is the point: making these rates *reasonable*, not esoteric.
:::

## 2. Gradient descent: convergence proved {#ch2}

This chapter answers the first question of the module: under which assumptions does gradient descent converge, and how fast? The algorithm is the most widely used one in machine learning:

$$x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\, \nabla f(x_k), \qquad \eta > 0 \text{ the step (learning rate).}$$

::: note
[Intuition first: the step on a one-dimensional quadratic]{.tag} Take $f(x) = \tfrac{L}{2}x^2$, whose gradient $Lx$ is exactly $L$-Lipschitz. One step gives
$$
x_{k+1} = (1 - \eta L)\,x_k .
$$

-   If $0 < \eta < 2/L$, then $|1 - \eta L| < 1$ and the iterates go to $0$;
-   the choice $\eta = 1/L$ reaches $0$ in a single step;
-   if $\eta > 2/L$, then $|1 - \eta L| > 1$ and the iterates oscillate with growing amplitude.

This is the oscillating loss of the introduction, explained: a step larger than $2/L$ along the steepest direction makes descent diverge, whatever happens elsewhere. All the results below assume $\eta \leq 1/L$, which leaves a safety factor of two.
:::

:::: prop
[Lemma 2.1 — Guaranteed descent (descent lemma)]{.tag} If $f$ is $L$-smooth and $0 < \eta \leq 1/L$:
$$
f(x_{k+1}) \;\leq\; f(x_k) - \tfrac{\eta}{2}\,\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2.
$$

::: proof
By the quadratic upper bound at $y = x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\nabla f(x_k)$:
$$
f(x_{k+1}) \leq f(x_k) + \langle\nabla f(x_k), -\eta\nabla f(x_k)\rangle + \tfrac{L}{2}\eta^2\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 = f(x_k) - \eta(1 - \tfrac{L\eta}{2})\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2,
$$
and $\eta(1-\tfrac{L\eta}{2}) \geq \tfrac{\eta}{2}$ whenever $\eta \leq 1/L$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.2 — $O(1/k)$ convergence (smooth convex case, proved)]{.tag} Let $f$ be convex and $L$-smooth, $x^\star$ a minimizer, $R = \|x_0 - x^\star\|$, $\eta = 1/L$. Then
$$
f(x_{k+1}) - f(x^\star) \;\leq\; \frac{L R^2}{2\,(k+1)}.
$$

::: proof
**Step 1 (three-point inequality).** For every $y$ — quadratic upper bound of $f$ at $x_k$ evaluated at $x_{k+1}$, combined with convexity $f(x_k) \leq f(y) + \langle\nabla f(x_k), x_k - y\rangle$ —:
$$
f(x_{k+1}) \;\leq\; f(y) + \langle\nabla f(x_k), x_{k+1} - y\rangle + \frac{L}{2}\|x_{k+1} - x_k\|^2.
$$

**Step 2 ($y = x^\star$ and polarization).** With $\nabla f(x_k) = L\,(x_k - x_{k+1})$ and $y = x^\star$, then the identity
$$
\langle a, b\rangle = \tfrac12(\|a+b\|^2 - \|a\|^2 - \|b\|^2)
$$
applied to $a = x_k - x_{k+1}$, $b = x_{k+1} - x^\star$ (so that $\|a+b\| = \|x_k - x^\star\| = R_k$):
$$
f(x_{k+1}) - f^\star \;\leq\; L\langle x_k - x_{k+1},\, x_{k+1} - x^\star\rangle + \frac{L}{2}\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2 \;=\; \frac{L}{2}\big(R_k^2 - R_{k+1}^2\big).
$$

**Step 3 (telescoping).** Summing from $0$ to $T-1$ and using $\|x_T - x^\star\|^2 \geq 0$:
$$
\sum_{k=0}^{T-1} (f(x_{k+1}) - f^\star) \leq \tfrac{L}{2}R_0^2 .
$$
Since the sequence $f(x_k)$ is decreasing (lemma 2.1), each term is bounded by the average:
$$
f(x_T) - f^\star \leq \tfrac{L R^2}{2T}.
$$
[∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 2.3 — Linear convergence ($\mu$-strongly convex case, proved)]{.tag} Let $f$ be $\mu$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth, $\eta = 1/L$. Then, with $\kappa = L/\mu$ the **condition number**:

::: key
[Key result — linear convergence of gradient descent]{.tag}
$$
f(x_{k+1}) - f(x^\star) \;\leq\; \Big(1 - \frac{1}{\kappa}\Big)\,\big(f(x_k) - f(x^\star)\big), \qquad f(x_k) - f^\star \;\leq\; e^{-k/\kappa}\,\big(f(x_0)-f^\star\big).
$$
:::

::: proof
Strong convexity implies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality, by minimizing over $x$ the quadratic lower bound
$$
f(x_k) + \langle\nabla f(x_k), x - x_k\rangle + \tfrac{\mu}{2}\|x - x_k\|^2 .
$$
The inequality reads:
$$
f(x_k) - f^\star \leq \tfrac{1}{2\mu}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2, \quad \text{i.e.} \quad \|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 \geq 2\mu\,(f(x_k)-f^\star).
$$
Injecting into lemma 2.1:
$$
f(x_{k+1}) \leq f(x_k) - \frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 \leq f(x_k) - \frac{\mu}{L}(f(x_k)-f^\star).
$$
The error decreases geometrically by the factor $1-\mu/L = 1-1/\kappa \leq e^{-1/\kappa}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[Reading the two rates — what $\kappa$ tells us]{.tag}

-   Merely convex: error in $1/k$ — to divide the error by 100, 100 more iterations.
-   Strongly convex: error in $(1-1/\kappa)^k \approx e^{-k/\kappa}$ — to gain a factor $e$, $\kappa$ iterations.

With $\kappa = 10^4$ (ill-conditioned regression, next chapter), it is night: the "basic" descent is *exponentially* penalized by the condition number.

Not optimal: for a quadratic, $\eta = 2/(\mu+L)$ yields the factor $\big(\tfrac{\kappa-1}{\kappa+1}\big)^2$ on the values (exercise 4): better, but still $O(\kappa)$. Breaking this barrier is the subject of chapter 3.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.4 — Counting iterations before running them]{.tag} A ridge regression has $L = 10$ and $\mu = 0.1$, so $\kappa = 100$. To divide the initial error $f(x_0) - f^\star$ by $10^6$, theorem 2.3 asks for $e^{-k/\kappa} \leq 10^{-6}$, i.e.
$$
k \geq \kappa \ln 10^6 \approx 1\,382 \text{ iterations.}
$$
Without the strong convexity (or ignoring it), theorem 2.2 only guarantees an error $LR^2/(2k)$: with $L = 10$, $R = 1$ and a target $10^{-6}$, it asks for
$$
k \geq 5 \times 10^6 \text{ iterations.}
$$
The two bounds differ by more than three orders of magnitude on the same problem, which is why identifying $\mu$ — for instance through an explicit $\ell_2$ penalty — is worth the effort.
:::

::: ex
[Example 2.5 — Seeing the condition number in two dimensions]{.tag} $f(u,v) = \tfrac{1}{2}(u^2 + \kappa v^2)$: $\kappa = L/\mu$ exactly, with $\nabla f = (u, \kappa v)$. At step $1/L = 1/\kappa$:

-   the *steep* direction $v$ is canceled in one iteration ($v_1 = v_0 - \tfrac{1}{\kappa}\kappa v_0 = 0$);
-   the *flat* direction $u$ decreases only by $(1-1/\kappa)$ per step: it — the elongated valley — sets the pace ($\kappa$ iterations).

As soon as the quadratic is rotated (axes not aligned), the trajectory zigzags across the valley. This is *the* plot to remember from the module: all the "loss landscape" figures of networks (see the Deep Learning module, ch. 3) show these valleys — hence momentum.
:::

```python
import numpy as np

def gradient_descent(grad, x0, step, n_iter=200):
    x, traj = x0.copy(), [x0.copy()]
    for _ in range(n_iter):
        x = x - step * grad(x)
        traj.append(x.copy())
    return np.array(traj)

kappa = 200.0
A = np.diag([1.0, kappa])          # L = kappa, mu = 1, condition number = kappa
grad = lambda x: A @ x
x0 = np.array([9.0, 0.0])          # start on the flat axis: the worst case
traj = gradient_descent(grad, x0, step=1.0/kappa)
err = 0.5 * np.sum(traj**2 * np.array([1.0, kappa]), axis=1)
print(err[-1] / err[0])   # (1 - 1/kappa)**400 ~ 0.135: slow!
# optimal step for a quadratic: 2/(mu + L)
traj_opt = gradient_descent(grad, x0, step=2.0/(1.0+kappa))
err_opt = 0.5 * np.sum(traj_opt**2 * np.array([1.0, kappa]), axis=1)
print(err_opt[-1] / err_opt[0])    # ((kappa-1)/(kappa+1))**400 ~ 0.018: better
# from (9, 9) instead, step 1/L kills the steep coordinate (which carries
# almost all of the initial error) in one step: the ratio then looks tiny
# (~7e-4) although the flat coordinate is just as slow
```

## 3. Conditioning and Nesterov acceleration {#ch3}

Gradient descent pays a factor $\kappa$ in iterations; this chapter asks whether another first-order method can pay less. Can we go faster *without second-order information* (no Hessian)? Nesterov's answer (1983): yes, by a factor $\sqrt{\kappa}$ — and this is **optimal**: no first-order algorithm can do better on the class of smooth convex functions. This is one of the rare results of the discipline where optimality is known *and* achieved by a usable algorithm.

::: thm
[Theorem 3.1 — First-order lower bound (Nesterov 1983; Nemirovski–Yudin 1983)]{.tag} For any first-order method (having access only to gradients at the visited points), there exists a $\mu$-strongly convex and $L$-smooth function such that, after $T$ iterations,
$$
f(x_T) - f(x^\star) \;\geq\; \Big(1 - \frac{1}{\sqrt{\kappa}}\Big)^{2T}\,\big(f(x_0)-f(x^\star)\big) \quad\text{(up to constants).}
$$
In other words:
$$
\Omega\!\big(\sqrt{\kappa}\,\log(1/\varepsilon)\big)
$$
iterations are necessary, versus $\Omega(\kappa \log(1/\varepsilon))$ for gradient descent; and $\Omega(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$ iterations in the general smooth convex case (vs $\Omega(1/\varepsilon)$).

The proofs construct a blockwise quadratic "trap function" whose information propagates only one coordinate per iteration: they can be found in Nesterov (2004, §2.1) and Bubeck (2015, §3.5).
:::

:::: def
[Definition 3.2 — Accelerated scheme (Nesterov, strongly convex case)]{.tag} With the momentum coefficient $\beta = \frac{1 - \sqrt{\mu/L}}{1 + \sqrt{\mu/L}}$ and step $\eta = 1/L$:

::: key
[Key result — Nesterov acceleration]{.tag}
$$
y_k = x_k + \beta\,(x_k - x_{k-1}), \qquad x_{k+1} = y_k - \eta\,\nabla f(y_k),
$$
:::

and the initialization $y_0 = x_0$. Convergence is linear with factor $1 - \sqrt{\mu/L} = 1 - 1/\sqrt{\kappa}$ — the promised $\sqrt{\kappa}$ factor.

"Smooth convex" variant: $\beta_k = \frac{k-1}{k+2}$ (growing momentum), rate
$$
f(x_k) - f^\star \leq \frac{2L\|x_0-x^\star\|^2}{(k+1)^2}.
$$
::::

::: ex
[Example 3.3 — What the factor $\sqrt{\kappa}$ buys]{.tag} On an ill-conditioned least-squares problem with $\kappa = 10^4$, dividing the error by $10^6$ costs

-   gradient descent about $\kappa \ln 10^6 \approx 1.4 \times 10^5$ iterations (theorem 2.3),
-   the accelerated scheme about $\sqrt{\kappa}\,\ln 10^6 \approx 1.4 \times 10^3$:

a hundred times fewer, for the same cost per iteration (one gradient and one extra vector addition).

The gain grows with $\kappa$, which is exactly when it is needed. The momentum coefficient here is
$$
\beta = \frac{1 - 1/\sqrt{\kappa}}{1 + 1/\sqrt{\kappa}} \approx 0.98 :
$$
almost all of the previous displacement is kept, which is what lets the iterates build up speed along the flat direction of the valley.
:::

::: thm
[Theorem 3.4 — Intuition of the proof: estimate sequences]{.tag} The idea (detailed in Nesterov 2004, §2.2), in the smooth convex case $\mu = 0$: build quadratic models
$$
\phi_k(x) = \phi_k^\star + \frac{\gamma_k}{2}\|x - v_k\|^2, \qquad \phi_0(x) = f(x_0) + \frac{L}{2}\|x - x_0\|^2,
$$
by mixing in, at each step, the linear lower bound of $f$ at a look-ahead point $y_k$:
$$
\phi_{k+1}(x) = (1-\alpha_k)\,\phi_k(x) + \alpha_k\Big(f(y_k) + \langle\nabla f(y_k), x - y_k\rangle\Big).
$$
Two properties are kept along the way.

1.  **The model is almost below $f$.** With $\lambda_k = \prod_{j<k}(1-\alpha_j)$, induction on the recursion gives, for every $x$,
    $$
    \phi_k(x) \leq (1-\lambda_k)\, f(x) + \lambda_k\, \phi_0(x).
    $$
2.  **The iterate beats the model.** The invariant is $f(x_k) \leq \phi_k^\star$, with $\phi_k^\star = \min \phi_k$. It is preserved when $y_k$ is the right convex combination of $x_k$ and $v_k$, and $x_{k+1} = y_k - \tfrac{1}{L}\nabla f(y_k)$.

Taking $x = x^\star$ in 1 and chaining with 2:
$$
f(x_k) - f^\star \;\leq\; \phi_k(x^\star) - f^\star \;\leq\; \lambda_k\big(\phi_0(x^\star) - f^\star\big) \;\leq\; \lambda_k\, L R^2 ,
$$
since smoothness gives $f(x_0) - f^\star \leq L R^2/2$.

The curvature of the models *decreases*, $\gamma_{k+1} = (1-\alpha_k)\gamma_k$. The weight $\alpha_k$ is the largest that the descent lemma allows:
$$
L\alpha_k^2 = \gamma_{k+1}.
$$
Since $\gamma_k = L\lambda_k$, this reads $\alpha_k^2 = \lambda_{k+1}$, which gives $\alpha_k \approx 2/k$ and $\lambda_k \leq 4/(k+2)^2$, hence
$$
f(x_k) - f^\star \leq \frac{4 L R^2}{(k+2)^2} = O(L R^2/k^2).
$$
In continuous time $t \approx k\sqrt{\eta}$ (Su, Boyd and Candès, 2016), the scheme becomes the ODE
$$
\ddot{x} + \tfrac{3}{t}\dot{x} + \nabla f(x) = 0
$$
— a ball in the valley with vanishing friction, along which $f(x(t)) - f^\star \leq 2R^2/t^2$: the signature of acceleration.
:::

::: note
[Momentum in practice: from Nesterov to PyTorch]{.tag}

| Variant | Update | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Heavy ball (Polyak 1964) | $v_{k+1} = \beta v_k - \eta\nabla f(x_k)$, $x_{k+1} = x_k + v_{k+1}$ | networks (SGD+momentum 0.9); optimal for quadratics, no general guarantee |
| Nesterov (this chapter) | gradient evaluated at the *future* point $y_k$ | optimal guarantees, FISTA (ch. 4), convex case |
| Adaptive restart (O'Donoghue–Candès 2015) | restart the momentum ($\beta_k$ back to $0$) when $f$ rises | practical twist: linearizes convergence of the strongly convex case without knowing $\mu$ |

The [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch3) module (section 3.2) shows, mode by mode on a quadratic, what heavy-ball momentum changes. This chapter adds why it matters: momentum, in Nesterov's form, is what reaches the $\sqrt{\kappa}$ factor that theorem 3.1 proves optimal on valleys of condition number $\kappa$.
:::

## 4. Proximal methods: ISTA and FISTA {#ch4}

This chapter extends gradient descent to objectives with a non-differentiable part. Gradient descent requires a gradient — impossible for $F = f + \lambda\|\theta\|_1$ at the points where a coordinate is zero. The proximal trick: handle the smooth part with a gradient step, the non-smooth part with an *explicit operation*.

::: def
[Definition 4.1 — Proximal operator]{.tag} For $g\colon \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}$ convex lower semi-continuous:
$$
\mathrm{prox}_{\eta g}(v) = \arg\min_x \;\Big\{ g(x) + \frac{1}{2\eta}\|x - v\|^2 \Big\}.
$$
Special cases:

-   $g = 0$ gives $v$ (gradient descent);
-   $g = \iota_C$ (indicator of a closed convex set $C$) gives the projection $\Pi_C(v)$;
-   $g = \lambda\|\cdot\|_1$ gives componentwise soft thresholding (example 1.4).
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 4.2 — Firm non-expansiveness (proved)]{.tag} For all $v, w$:
$$
\|\mathrm{prox}_{\eta g}(v) - \mathrm{prox}_{\eta g}(w)\| \;\leq\; \|v - w\|.
$$

::: proof
Write $p = \mathrm{prox}_{\eta g}(v)$, $q = \mathrm{prox}_{\eta g}(w)$. The optimality condition 1.3 gives $0 \in \partial g(p) + \tfrac{1}{\eta}(p - v)$ and $0 \in \partial g(q) + \tfrac{1}{\eta}(q-w)$, that is $\tfrac{1}{\eta}(v - p) \in \partial g(p)$ and $\tfrac{1}{\eta}(w-q) \in \partial g(q)$.

Monotonicity of the subdifferential ($\langle u - u', x - x'\rangle \geq 0$ for $u \in \partial g(x)$, $u' \in \partial g(x')$) yields
$$
\langle (v-p) - (w-q),\, p - q\rangle \geq 0, \quad \text{i.e.} \quad \langle v - w, p - q\rangle \geq \|p-q\|^2.
$$
By Cauchy–Schwarz, $\|v-w\| \geq \|p-q\|$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

:::: def
[Definition 4.3 — ISTA and FISTA (Beck–Teboulle 2009; Daubechies et al. 2004)]{.tag} **ISTA** (iterative shrinkage-thresholding):

::: key
[Key result — the proximal gradient step]{.tag}
$$
x_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{\eta g}\big(x_k - \eta\,\nabla f(x_k)\big), \qquad \eta \leq 1/L.
$$
:::

**FISTA** (fast ISTA): ISTA + the Nesterov acceleration stage —
$$
y_k = x_k + \frac{k-1}{k+2}\,(x_k - x_{k-1}), \qquad x_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{\eta g}\big(y_k - \eta\,\nabla f(y_k)\big).
$$
::::

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.4 — Rates of ISTA and FISTA (proved)]{.tag} Let $F = f + g$ with $f$ convex $L$-smooth and $g$ convex, and let $R = \|x_0 - x^\star\|$. ISTA at step $1/L$ satisfies
$$
F(x_k) - F(x^\star) \;\leq\; \frac{L R^2}{2k}.
$$
FISTA achieves
$$
F(x_k) - F(x^\star) \leq \frac{2L R^2}{(k+1)^2}
$$
— the $\sqrt{\cdot}$ factor gained on the iteration count, exactly as in chapter 3.

::: proof
Take $\eta = 1/L$, set $u_k = x_k - \tfrac{1}{L}\nabla f(x_k)$ and $x_{k+1} = \mathrm{prox}_{g/L}(u_k)$, the minimizer of $\phi(x) = g(x) + \tfrac{L}{2}\|x - u_k\|^2$.

1.  **Proximal inequality.** The function $\phi$ is $L$-strongly convex and minimized at $x_{k+1}$, so for every $y$:
    $$
    \phi(y) \geq \phi(x_{k+1}) + \tfrac{L}{2}\|y - x_{k+1}\|^2 .
    $$
    Expanding
    $$
    \|y - u_k\|^2 = \|y - x_k\|^2 + \tfrac{2}{L}\langle \nabla f(x_k), y - x_k\rangle + \tfrac{1}{L^2}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2,
    $$
    and the same for $x_{k+1}$, the gradient-norm terms cancel and we get
    $$
    g(x_{k+1}) \;\leq\; g(y) + \langle \nabla f(x_k),\, y - x_{k+1}\rangle + \frac{L}{2}\Big(\|y - x_k\|^2 - \|y - x_{k+1}\|^2 - \|x_{k+1} - x_k\|^2\Big).
    $$
2.  **Smoothness, then convexity of $f$.**
    $$
    f(x_{k+1}) \leq f(x_k) + \langle\nabla f(x_k), x_{k+1}-x_k\rangle + \tfrac{L}{2}\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2 \quad \text{and} \quad f(x_k) \leq f(y) + \langle \nabla f(x_k), x_k - y\rangle,
    $$
    whose sum is
    $$
    f(x_{k+1}) \leq f(y) + \langle\nabla f(x_k), x_{k+1} - y\rangle + \tfrac{L}{2}\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2 .
    $$
3.  **Sum of 1 and 2.** The inner products and the terms $\|x_{k+1}-x_k\|^2$ cancel:
    $$
    F(x_{k+1}) \;\leq\; F(y) + \frac{L}{2}\Big(\|y - x_k\|^2 - \|y - x_{k+1}\|^2\Big) \qquad \text{for every } y.
    $$
4.  **Telescoping.** With $y = x_k$ this shows that $F(x_k)$ is non-increasing. With $y = x^\star$ and summing from $0$ to $k-1$, the right-hand side telescopes:
    $$
    \sum_{j=1}^{k} \big(F(x_j) - F^\star\big) \leq \tfrac{L}{2}\|x_0 - x^\star\|^2 .
    $$
    Since the terms decrease, the last one is at most their average: $F(x_k) - F^\star \leq \frac{LR^2}{2k}$ — the same telescoping as in theorem 2.2.

*FISTA* (Beck–Teboulle 2009, th. 4.4). Write the momentum of definition 4.3 as $(t_k - 1)/t_{k+1}$ with $t_k = (k+1)/2$. The proof only uses three properties of the sequence:
$$
t_1 = 1, \qquad t_{k+1}^2 - t_{k+1} \leq t_k^2, \qquad t_k \geq \tfrac{k+1}{2}.
$$
Beck and Teboulle's $t_{k+1} = \big(1 + \sqrt{1 + 4t_k^2}\big)/2$, used in the code of example 4.5, has them too.

5.  **Step 3 from any point.** Steps 1–3 never used that the gradient step starts at $x_k$. Started at $y_k$, as in FISTA, they give for every $z$:
    $$
    F(x_{k+1}) \;\leq\; F(z) + \frac{L}{2}\Big(\|z - y_k\|^2 - \|z - x_{k+1}\|^2\Big).
    $$
6.  **A moving comparison point.** Take $z = (1 - 1/t_{k+1})\,x_k + x^\star/t_{k+1}$. Convexity of $F$ gives
    $$
    F(z) - F^\star \leq \Big(1 - \frac{1}{t_{k+1}}\Big)\big(F(x_k) - F^\star\big).
    $$
    Set $w_k = t_k x_k - (t_k - 1)\,x_{k-1} - x^\star$. The formula for $y_k$ gives exactly
    $$
    z - y_k = -\frac{w_k}{t_{k+1}}, \qquad z - x_{k+1} = -\frac{w_{k+1}}{t_{k+1}}.
    $$
7.  **An energy that never increases.** Write $\delta_k = F(x_k) - F^\star$. Insert 6 into 5, multiply by $t_{k+1}^2$ and use $t_{k+1}^2 - t_{k+1} \leq t_k^2$:
    $$
    t_{k+1}^2\,\delta_{k+1} + \frac{L}{2}\|w_{k+1}\|^2 \;\leq\; t_k^2\,\delta_k + \frac{L}{2}\|w_k\|^2 .
    $$
8.  **Conclusion.** The first step starts from $y_0 = x_0$, and $t_1 = 1$ makes the comparison point $z = x^\star$, so step 5 gives
    $$
    t_1^2\,\delta_1 + \frac{L}{2}\|w_1\|^2 \leq \frac{L}{2}R^2 .
    $$
    The energy then never increases, so $t_k^2\,\delta_k \leq LR^2/2$. With $t_k \geq (k+1)/2$, this is the announced $F(x_k) - F^\star \leq 2LR^2/(k+1)^2$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.5 — LASSO: ISTA vs FISTA in practice]{.tag}

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d, s = 60, 200, 8                       # underdetermined, sparse support
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d)); X /= np.sqrt(n)
theta_true = np.zeros(d); theta_true[:s] = rng.normal(size=s)
y = X @ theta_true + 0.05 * rng.normal(size=n)

L = np.linalg.norm(X, 2) ** 2              # Lipschitz constant of f = 0.5||Xt-y||^2
lam = 0.1 * np.linalg.norm(X.T @ y, np.inf)

def soft(v, t): return np.sign(v) * np.maximum(np.abs(v) - t, 0)

def ista(x, iters):
    for _ in range(iters):
        x = soft(x - (1/L) * X.T @ (X @ x - y), lam/L)
    return x

def fista(x, iters):
    z, t = x.copy(), 1.0
    for k in range(1, iters+1):
        xn = soft(z - (1/L) * X.T @ (X @ z - y), lam/L)
        t_next = (1 + np.sqrt(1 + 4*t*t)) / 2
        z = xn + ((t-1)/t_next) * (xn - x)   # Nesterov momentum
        x, t = xn, t_next
    return x

F = lambda th: 0.5*np.sum((X@th - y)**2) + lam*np.abs(th).sum()
x0 = np.zeros(d)
F_ref = F(fista(x0.copy(), 5000))          # reference optimal value
for it in (20, 100):
    print(it, "ISTA gap:", F(ista(x0.copy(), it)) - F_ref,
              "FISTA gap:", F(fista(x0.copy(), it)) - F_ref)
# observed: FISTA's gap is ~50x smaller at 20 iterations, ~270x at 100;
# by 1000 iterations both reach machine precision
```

The $1/k^2$ vs $1/k$ factor is visible in the first hundred iterations: same computations per iteration, radically different horizons. Later both methods converge linearly, faster than either guarantee, because this LASSO is strongly convex on the support of its solution (exercise 2 exploits this with a restart). This is also the foundation of compressed sensing solvers and of large-scale LASSO (see the Machine Learning module, ch. 2).
:::

::: note
[Beyond: ADMM in one sentence]{.tag} When even $f$ decomposes badly ($f = f_1 + f_2$ with two easy proxes but coupled variables), the ADMM method inherits $O(1/k)$ rates and reigns over problems with massive constraints. Its principle is augmented duality:

1.  rewrite $\min f_1(x) + f_2(z)$ subject to $x = z$;
2.  alternate a prox over $x$, a prox over $z$, a dual step on the multiplier.

The loop is closed with ch. 0: this is applied duality, hence the augmented Lagrangian — see ch. 8.
:::

### Non-smooth objectives without a prox: the subgradient method

The proximal methods above need $g$ to have a computable prox. When the whole objective is non-smooth and has no easy prox — a hinge loss summed over many points, a maximum of many affine functions — the only first-order information left is a subgradient (definition 1.2). The subgradient method simply follows it:
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta_k v_k \quad \text{with} \quad v_k \in \partial F(x_k).
$$
It is not a descent method, since a subgradient step can increase $F$, so the analysis tracks the distance to the solution instead of the function value.

:::: thm
[Theorem 4.6 — Rate of the subgradient method (proved)]{.tag} Let $F$ be convex with subgradients bounded by $G$, i.e. $F$ is $G$-Lipschitz:
$$
\|v\| \leq G \quad \text{for every } v \in \partial F(x).
$$
Let $x^\star$ be a minimizer and $R = \|x_0 - x^\star\|$. With the constant step $\eta = \frac{R}{G\sqrt{K}}$,
$$
\min_{0 \leq k < K}\; F(x_k) - F(x^\star) \;\leq\; \frac{R\,G}{\sqrt{K}}.
$$
The rate $1/\sqrt{K}$ is much slower than the $1/K$ of ISTA: dividing the error by $10$ costs $100$ times more iterations.

It cannot be improved in general: for $G$-Lipschitz convex functions, no first-order method does better than order $RG/\sqrt{K}$ when the dimension exceeds the number of iterations (Nemirovski–Yudin 1983).

::: proof
Expand the square and use the subgradient inequality $F(x^\star) \geq F(x_k) + \langle v_k, x^\star - x_k\rangle$:
$$
\|x_{k+1} - x^\star\|^2 = \|x_k - x^\star\|^2 - 2\eta\langle v_k, x_k - x^\star\rangle + \eta^2\|v_k\|^2 \leq \|x_k - x^\star\|^2 - 2\eta\big(F(x_k) - F(x^\star)\big) + \eta^2 G^2.
$$
Summing over $k = 0, \dots, K-1$, the distances telescope and the last one is non-negative:
$$
2\eta\sum_{k<K}\big(F(x_k) - F(x^\star)\big) \leq R^2 + K \eta^2 G^2 .
$$
The minimum is at most the average, so
$$
\min_k F(x_k) - F(x^\star) \leq \frac{R^2 + K \eta^2 G^2}{2\eta K}.
$$
With $\eta = R/(G\sqrt{K})$ both terms equal $\frac{RG}{2\sqrt{K}}$, which gives the bound. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 4.7 — Why the step must shrink: $F(x) = |x|$]{.tag} Start from $x_0 = 1$ with the constant step $\eta = 0.3$. The subgradient is the sign of $x$, so the iterates are
$$
0.7,\ 0.4,\ 0.1,\ -0.2,\ 0.1,\ -0.2,\ \dots
$$
They never reach $0$ and oscillate forever at a distance of order $\eta$, with $\min_k F(x_k) = 0.1$.

Theorem 4.6 explains this: with a constant step, the method only reaches a neighbourhood whose size is proportional to $\eta$, the same phenomenon as the SGD plateau of chapter 5.

Compare the proximal point method, which applies the prox of $\eta|x|$ (soft thresholding by $\eta$) at every step:
$$
1 \to 0.7 \to 0.4 \to 0.1 \to 0,
$$
exactly $0$ after four steps and forever after. Using the structure of the non-smooth term, when a prox is available, is what turns $1/\sqrt{K}$ into $1/K$.
:::

## 5. Stochastic gradient descent {#ch5}

This chapter analyses what happens when the gradient is replaced by a cheap, noisy estimate. When $n = 10^9$, computing $\nabla f$ costs $10^9$ evaluations — per iteration. The founding gesture of modern learning (Robbins–Monro, 1951): accept a *noisy but cheap* gradient.

::: def
[Definition 5.1 — SGD and assumptions]{.tag} Write the objective as $f = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n f_i$, where $f_i$ is the loss on sample $i$, plus the penalty when there is one, seen as a function of the parameter $x$. Draw an index $i_k$ uniformly at random (or a mini-batch):
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta_k\, g_k, \qquad g_k = \nabla f_{i_k}(x_k).
$$
Assumptions:

-   (H1) unbiasedness $\mathbb{E}[g_k \mid x_k] = \nabla f(x_k)$;
-   (H2) bounded variance $\mathbb{E}\|g_k - \nabla f(x_k)\|^2 \leq \sigma^2$;
-   (H3) Robbins–Monro $\sum \eta_k = \infty$, $\sum \eta_k^2 < \infty$ for decreasing steps.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.2 — What can be proved simply (proof)]{.tag} Let $f$ be convex $L$-smooth, (H1)–(H2), constant step $\eta \leq 1/L$. Then

::: key
[Key result — SGD at constant step]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[f(x_{k+1})\big] \;\leq\; \mathbb{E}\big[f(x_k)\big] - \frac{\eta}{2}\,\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 + \frac{\eta^2 L \sigma^2}{2}.
$$
:::

Consequences:

1.  the gradients become small on average:
    $$
    \liminf \mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 \leq L\sigma^2\eta ;
    $$
2.  if moreover $f$ is $\mu$-strongly convex, at constant step SGD converges to a **neighborhood** of the solution, not to the solution (exercise 6):
    $$
    \limsup_k \mathbb{E}[f(x_k)] - f^\star \leq \frac{\eta L\sigma^2}{2\mu} = O(\eta\sigma^2).
    $$

::: proof
Conditionally on $x_k$, the mean step equals $-\eta\nabla f(x_k)$ (unbiasedness) and the noise $\zeta_k = g_k - \nabla f(x_k)$ is centered. The descent lemma 2.1 applied to $x_k - \eta g_k$, then expanding the squares:
$$
\mathbb{E}_k[f(x_{k+1})] \leq f(x_k) - \eta\big(1 - \tfrac{L\eta}{2}\big)\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 + \tfrac{L\eta^2}{2}\,\mathbb{E}_k\|\zeta_k\|^2 \leq f(x_k) - \tfrac{\eta}{2}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 + \tfrac{L\eta^2\sigma^2}{2}.
$$
Consequence 1 follows by summing and using the bounded decrease of the errors. Consequence 2 injects the Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality of ch. 2, which strong convexity provides, and takes the fixed point of the resulting recursion. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

| Regime | Setting | Speed | Destination |
|---|---|---|---|
| decreasing $\eta_k \sim 1/\sqrt{k}$, averaged iterate | convex; violates (H3), since $\sum 1/k = \infty$ | $O(1/\sqrt{k})$ on the values | converges in value |
| decreasing $\eta_k \sim 1/(\mu k)$ | strongly convex; satisfies (H3) | $O(1/k)$ | converges to $x^\star$ |
| constant $\eta$ | practice (deep learning) | linear until the plateau | neighborhood $O(\eta\sigma^2)$ |
| constant + averaging (Polyak–Ruppert), $\bar{x}_k = \frac{1}{k}\sum x_j$ | least squares | $O(1/k)$, statistically optimal | converges to $x^\star$; otherwise to a point at distance $O(\eta)$ (ch. 11) |

::: ex
[Example 5.3 — The plateau computed exactly in one dimension]{.tag} Take $f(x) = \tfrac12 x^2$ (so $L = \mu = 1$) and a stochastic gradient $g_k = x_k + \xi_k$, where the noises $\xi_k$ are independent, centred, of variance $\sigma^2$. Constant-step SGD reads
$$
x_{k+1} = (1 - \eta)\,x_k - \eta\,\xi_k .
$$
Taking the expectation of the square, and using that $\xi_k$ is independent of $x_k$:
$$
\mathbb{E}[x_{k+1}^2] = (1-\eta)^2\,\mathbb{E}[x_k^2] + \eta^2\sigma^2.
$$
For $0 < \eta < 2$ this linear recursion converges to its fixed point
$$
s = \eta^2\sigma^2/(1 - (1-\eta)^2) = \eta\sigma^2/(2 - \eta).
$$
Hence, for small $\eta$,
$$
\mathbb{E}[f(x_k)] \to \frac{\eta\sigma^2}{2(2-\eta)} \approx \frac{\eta\sigma^2}{4} :
$$
the plateau is proportional to the step, as theorem 5.2 announced (exercise 6 gives the general bound $\frac{\eta L\sigma^2}{2\mu}$, here $\frac{\eta\sigma^2}{2}$, larger by a factor of two only).

The transient, on the other hand, decays like $(1-\eta)^{2k}$: halving the step halves the plateau but doubles the number of iterations needed to reach it. Decreasing step schedules are the systematic way out of this trade-off.
:::

::: note
[Minibatching: buying variance with compute]{.tag} A mini-batch $B$ of size $b$ replaces $g_k$ with the average over $B$: the variance drops to $\sigma^2/b$ (independent draws), the cost rises to $b$ gradients.

At a fixed compute budget, large $b$ = less noise but fewer steps — the optimal trade-off depends on the regime: in the convex case, steps of modest size $b$ often dominate (Bottou–Curtis–Nocedal 2018, §5.3); in deep learning, very large batches require correcting the step (LARS, ch. 10). Hence the question of the next chapter: can we kill the variance *without* paying $b$ or $n$ at every step?
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 5.4 — Noise is not (only) an evil]{.tag} The stationary regime $O(\eta\sigma^2)$ of theorem 5.2 has a positive side: the fluctuations around the minimum sweep the "passes" of the landscape and experience (see the Deep Learning module, ch. 3) shows that the "flat" minima found by SGD often generalize better than the narrow valleys reached by deterministic methods. The very sigma² that sets the stationary error acts as an implicit regularizer — an active research theme (see ch. 11, A. Dieuleveut's work on constant-step SGD).
:::

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n, d = 20_000, 50
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d)) / np.sqrt(d)
y = (X @ rng.normal(size=d) + 0.3*rng.normal(size=n) > 0).astype(float)  # labels in {0, 1}

def sgd_logreg(eta, epochs=20, b=32):
    w = np.zeros(d); losses = []
    sig = lambda z: 1/(1+np.exp(-z))
    for ep in range(epochs):
        idx = rng.permutation(n)
        for s in range(0, n, b):
            B = idx[s:s+b]
            p = sig(X[B] @ w)
            g = X[B].T @ (p - y[B]) / b      # mini-batch gradient
            w = w - eta * g
        losses.append(np.mean(np.logaddexp(0, -(2*y-1)*(X@w))))  # full training risk
    return losses

# here L ~ 0.005 (features scaled by 1/sqrt(d)): all three steps are below 1/L
for eta in (0.1, 1.0, 100.0):
    print(eta, "->", sgd_logreg(eta)[-1])
# observed (optimal risk 0.200): 0.255 (too small, still descending),
# 0.201 (near the optimum), 0.26 (noisy plateau: the eta*sigma^2 term)
```

### SGD without convexity: approximate stationary points

Neural network losses are not convex, so the convex rates above do not apply to them. What remains provable is weaker but useful: SGD finds a point where the gradient is small. The inequality of theorem 5.2 never used convexity — only $L$-smoothness, unbiasedness and bounded variance — so it can be summed directly.

:::: thm
[Theorem 5.5 — Non-convex SGD (Ghadimi–Lan 2013, proved)]{.tag} Let $f$ be $L$-smooth (not necessarily convex) and bounded below by $f_{\inf}$, let (H1)–(H2) hold and set $\Delta = f(x_0) - f_{\inf}$. With a constant step $\eta \leq 1/L$,
$$
\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1} \mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 \;\leq\; \frac{2\Delta}{\eta K} + \eta L \sigma^2.
$$
With
$$
\eta = \min\big(1/L,\ \sqrt{2\Delta/(L\sigma^2 K)}\big),
$$
the right-hand side is at most $2\sqrt{2\Delta L\sigma^2/K}$ when the second term of the minimum is the active one: an iterate drawn uniformly among $x_0, \dots, x_{K-1}$ has
$$
\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f\|^2 = O(1/\sqrt{K}).
$$

::: proof
Take the expectation of the inequality of theorem 5.2:
$$
\mathbb{E}f(x_{k+1}) \leq \mathbb{E}f(x_k) - \frac{\eta}{2}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 + \frac{L\eta^2\sigma^2}{2}.
$$
Summing over $k = 0, \dots, K-1$, the values telescope:
$$
\frac{\eta}{2}\sum_{k<K}\mathbb{E}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 \leq f(x_0) - \mathbb{E}f(x_K) + \frac{KL\eta^2\sigma^2}{2} \leq \Delta + \frac{KL\eta^2\sigma^2}{2},
$$
since $f(x_K) \geq f_{\inf}$. Dividing by $K\eta/2$ gives the bound. For the step choice, $\eta = \sqrt{2\Delta/(L\sigma^2K)}$ makes the two terms equal, each to $\sqrt{2\Delta L\sigma^2/K}$. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 5.6 — Reading the non-convex bound]{.tag} Take $\Delta = 1$, $L = 10$, $\sigma^2 = 1$ and $K = 10^4$ steps. The tuned step is
$$
\eta = \sqrt{2/(10 \cdot 10^4)} \approx 4.5 \times 10^{-3},
$$
below $1/L = 0.1$, and the bound on the average squared gradient norm is
$$
2\sqrt{2 \cdot 10/10^4} \approx 0.089 .
$$
Dividing this bound by $10$ requires $100$ times more steps.

Two cautions: the guarantee is on the average (or on a randomly chosen iterate), not on the last one; and a small gradient certifies a stationary point, which may be a saddle point or a poor local minimum. Chapter 10 discusses why, for neural networks, this weak guarantee is nevertheless what one observes in practice.
:::

## 6. Variance reduction: SAGA and SVRG {#ch6}

This chapter removes the plateau of constant-step SGD without paying a full gradient at every step. Between the "complete but expensive" and the "stochastic but noisy" gradient, a third way: keep **memory** of past gradients to build an unbiased estimator whose variance vanishes by itself.

::: def
[Definition 6.1 — SAGA (Defazio, Bach, Lacoste-Julien, 2014)]{.tag} One maintains a table $\phi_i \approx \nabla f_i(x)$ of the latest gradient computed for each term, and $\bar\phi = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \phi_i$. At each iteration, draw $i$ and step with the *stored* $\phi_i$ and $\bar\phi$:
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\Big(\nabla f_i(x_k) - \phi_i + \bar\phi\Big);
$$
only then set $\phi_i \leftarrow \nabla f_i(x_k)$ and update $\bar\phi$. The estimator is unbiased, because the stored table does not depend on the current draw; updating the table first would cancel $\nabla f_i(x_k) - \phi_i$ and leave the biased step $-\eta\bar\phi$. Its variance is at most
$$
\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \|\nabla f_i(x_k) - \phi_i\|^2 \to 0
$$
at convergence — instead of SGD's permanent $\sigma^2$.
:::

::: def
[Definition 6.2 — SVRG (Johnson–Zhang, 2013)]{.tag} Without a table: every $m$ steps, recompute a full gradient $\tilde\nabla = \nabla f(\tilde{x})$ at a "viewpoint" $\tilde x$ (snapshot), then use
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\Big(\nabla f_i(x_k) - \nabla f_i(\tilde x) + \tilde\nabla\Big).
$$
Also unbiased; variance $\propto \|\nabla f_i(x_k) - \nabla f_i(\tilde x)\|^2$, small when $x_k$ stays near the snapshot. Memory cost: $O(d)$ — the big industrial argument.
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 6.3 — Linear convergence (statement, sketch)]{.tag} For $f = \frac{1}{n}\sum f_i$ $\mu$-strongly convex, each $f_i$ $L$-smooth, SAGA and SVRG with step $\eta \asymp 1/L$ converge *linearly*:

::: key
[Key result — variance reduction]{.tag}
$$
\mathbb{E}\big[F(x_k) - F(x^\star)\big] \;\leq\; \Big(1 - c\,\min\Big(\frac{1}{n}, \frac{\mu}{L}\Big)\Big)^{k}\,\big(F(x_0)-F(x^\star)\big),
$$
:::

that is $O\big((n + \kappa)\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\big)$ evaluations of individual gradients — versus $O(n\kappa\log\frac{1}{\varepsilon})$ for deterministic descent.

For $n = 10^5$ examples and $\kappa = 10^3$, this is $1.01 \times 10^5$ against $10^8$ gradient evaluations per factor $e$ of accuracy: about a thousand times fewer.

*Sketch.* The proof couples two recurrences: the decrease in function value (as in ch. 2, via unbiasedness) and the decrease of the estimator's variance (extra contraction provided by the table/snapshot); the variance becoming multiplicative, it converts SGD's $O(\eta\sigma^2)$ plateau into a geometric contraction. [∎]{.qed}
::::

  Method                   Gradient/iteration   Memory             Evaluations for $\varepsilon$ (strongly convex)
  ------------------------ -------------------- ------------------ -------------------------------------------------------------------
  GD (ch. 2)               $n$                  $O(d)$             $O(n\,\kappa \log 1/\varepsilon)$
  AGD (ch. 3)              $n$                  $O(d)$             $O(n\,\sqrt{\kappa} \log 1/\varepsilon)$
  SGD (ch. 5)              1                    $O(d)$             $O\big(\sigma^2/(\mu^2\varepsilon)\big)$ — not linear
  SAGA / SVRG (this ch.)   1 (+$n$ every $m$)   $O(nd)$ / $O(d)$   $O\big((n+\kappa)\log 1/\varepsilon\big)$
  SVRG + acceleration      1                    $O(d)$             $O\big(n + \sqrt{n\kappa}\big)\log 1/\varepsilon$ — optimal

::: note
[Where theory stops (and deep learning begins)]{.tag} In deep learning, $f_i$ is not convex, the SAGA table explodes ($n$ gradient-sized models), and SGD noise is an ally (prop. 5.4): strict variance reduction is little used there. But the *structure* of the trade-off — variance vs cost per iteration — governs the batch choices, step schedules and Adam variants (ch. 10). Convex theory is the compass, not the territory.
:::

## 7. Newton and quasi-Newton {#ch7}

First-order methods pay for the condition number $\kappa$; this chapter buys second-order information (the Hessian) to remove it. The reward is *quadratic* local convergence — the number of correct digits *doubles* at every iteration — and the price is the cost of each iteration.

:::: thm
[Theorem 7.1 — Local quadratic convergence (proved)]{.tag} Let $f$ be twice differentiable, $\mu I \preceq \nabla^2 f(x) \preceq LI$ everywhere ($f$ therefore strongly convex), Hessian $M$-Lipschitz. Newton's method
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - \nabla^2 f(x_k)^{-1} \nabla f(x_k)
$$
satisfies, as soon as $\|x_0 - x^\star\| \leq \mu/M$:

::: key
[Key result — quadratic convergence of Newton's method]{.tag}
$$
\|x_{k+1} - x^\star\| \;\leq\; \frac{M}{2\mu}\,\|x_k - x^\star\|^2.
$$
:::

::: proof
Write $e_k = x_k - x^\star$ and expand $\nabla f$ at $x_k$ around $x^\star$ (where $\nabla f(x^\star) = 0$):
$$
0 = \nabla f(x^\star) = \nabla f(x_k) - \int_0^1 \nabla^2 f(x^\star + s e_k)\, e_k \, ds \;\Rightarrow\; \nabla f(x_k) = H_k e_k - \rho_k,\quad \|\rho_k\| \leq \frac{M}{2}\|e_k\|^2,
$$
where $H_k = \nabla^2 f(x_k)$ and
$$
\rho_k = \int_0^1 (H_k - \nabla^2 f(x^\star+se_k))e_k\,ds
$$
collects the Hessian gap ($\leq M \|e_k\|$ in operator norm, hence the $\tfrac{M}{2}\|e_k\|^2$ after integration). Then
$$
e_{k+1} = e_k - H_k^{-1}\nabla f(x_k) = H_k^{-1}\rho_k \;\Rightarrow\; \|e_{k+1}\| \leq \|H_k^{-1}\| \,\frac{M}{2}\|e_k\|^2 \leq \frac{M}{2\mu}\|e_k\|^2.
$$
If $\|e_0\| \leq \mu/M$, the error at least halves at every step — and then decreases quadratically once below 1. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: note
[The price to pay — and the workaround]{.tag}

|  | GD / Nesterov | Newton | BFGS / L-BFGS |
|---|---|---|---|
| cost per iteration (dimension $d$) | $O(d)$ | $O(d^3)$ (factorization) | $O(d^2)$ / $O(md)$, $m \approx 10$ |
| information | gradients | full Hessian | approximation from gradient differences |
| convergence | global, linear/$k^2$ | local quadratic | superlinear (in practice: fast linear) |
| scale invariance | no (suffers from $\kappa$) | yes (affine invariant) | almost |

Newton is not global: far from the minimum, the direction can be bad — hence *damped Newton* (step by line search) and the "self-concordant" analysis (Nesterov–Nemirovski) which gives a globally convergent version; this is the heart of interior-point LP/QP solvers (the linear programs of the Responsible AI module, ch. 4, if you took it in P1).
:::

::: def
[Definition 7.2 — BFGS in three ideas]{.tag}

1.  **Goal**: replace $\nabla^2 f$ with $B_k \succ 0$ updated at cost $O(d^2)$.
2.  **Secant equation**: impose $B_{k+1} s_k = y_k$ with $s_k = x_{k+1}-x_k$, $y_k = \nabla f(x_{k+1})-\nabla f(x_k)$ — the only second-order information extractable from gradients.
3.  **Rank-2 update** (closest to $B_k$ in the Frobenius sense under these constraints):
    $$
    B_{k+1} = B_k - \frac{B_k s_k s_k^\top B_k}{s_k^\top B_k s_k} + \frac{y_k y_k^\top}{y_k^\top s_k}.
    $$

**L-BFGS** stores only the last $m$ pairs $(s_k, y_k)$ and reconstructs the product $B_k^{-1}\nabla f$ by recursion: it is the standard weapon for smooth convex losses in high dimension (and the default solver of `scipy.optimize.minimize(method="L-BFGS-B")`).
:::

::: ex
[Example 7.3 — Quadratic speed, experienced]{.tag} Minimize $f(x) = x\log x$ on $x > 0$, a convex function with $f'(x) = \log x + 1$ and $f''(x) = 1/x$; the minimizer is $x^\star = 1/e \approx 0.367879$. The Newton step simplifies to
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - f'(x_k)/f''(x_k) = -x_k \log x_k .
$$
From $x_0 = 0.5$ the errors $|x_k - x^\star|$ are
$$
1.3 \times 10^{-1},\quad 2.1 \times 10^{-2},\quad 6.3 \times 10^{-4},\quad 5.4 \times 10^{-7},\quad 3.9 \times 10^{-13}:
$$
the exponent roughly doubles at each step.

The ratio $|e_{k+1}|/e_k^2$ settles at about $1.36$, which is the constant $|f^{(3)}(x^\star)|/(2f''(x^\star)) = e/2$ predicted by a second-order expansion — the one-dimensional version of the constant $M/(2\mu)$ of theorem 7.1. Exercise 8 shows the counter-example: when $f''(x^\star) = 0$, as for $x^4$, the convergence is only linear.
:::

::: note
[Common mistakes with Newton's method]{.tag}

1.  Inverting the Hessian explicitly: one solves the linear system $\nabla^2 f(x_k)\, d = -\nabla f(x_k)$ by a Cholesky factorization, which is cheaper and more stable.
2.  Using the full step far from the minimum: without a line search, Newton can diverge even on a strictly convex function (try $f(x) = \sqrt{1 + x^2}$ from $x_0 = 2$: the iterates are $x_{k+1} = -x_k^3$).
3.  Applying it to a non-convex function without safeguard: where the Hessian has negative eigenvalues, the Newton direction can point uphill.
:::

## 8. Constraints in machine learning {#ch8}

This chapter shows how to train a model that must satisfy requirements, not only minimize an average loss. A real specification reads "error rate $\leq 5\,\%$ *and* demographic disparity $\leq \delta$ *and* latency $\leq 100$ ms". The average loss alone cannot express such **requirements**; constraints are needed — and hence the duality of ch. 0, applied.

::: def
[Definition 8.1 — Learning under constraints]{.tag}
$$
\min_{\theta}\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_i \ell(h_\theta(x_i), y_i) \quad\text{subject to}\quad \frac{1}{n}\sum_i c_j(h_\theta(x_i), x_i) \leq 0, \quad j = 1, \dots, m.
$$
Examples: demographic parity (gap of positive rates between groups), memory/latency budget at inference, false-negative rate in health. The empirical Lagrangian $\mathcal{L}(\theta,\lambda)$ and the dual $\max_{\lambda \geq 0} d(\lambda)$ are formed as in ch. 0.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 8.2 — Three ways to handle a constraint (compared)]{.tag}

| Technique | Problem solved | Advantage | Limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| quadratic penalty | $\min f + \tfrac{\rho}{2}\|g(\theta)_+\|^2$ | simple, smooth | residual violation $O(1/\rho)$; $\rho \to \infty$ stiffens the problem |
| projection (ch. 4) | $x_{k+1} = \Pi_\mathcal{C}(x_k - \eta\nabla f(x_k))$ | simple constraints (boxes, balls, simplices) | requires an exact projection |
| primal-dual (Uzawa) | $\theta_{k+1}$ minimizes $\mathcal{L}(\cdot, \lambda_k)$; $\lambda_{k+1} = [\lambda_k + \rho\, g(\theta_{k+1})]_+$ | general constraints, learns the price $\lambda$ | two step sizes to tune |
:::

:::: thm
[Theorem 8.3 — Projected gradient descent (proved)]{.tag} For $f$ convex $L$-smooth and $\mathcal{C}$ closed convex, the iteration
$$
x_{k+1} = \Pi_\mathcal{C}(x_k - \eta\nabla f(x_k)), \qquad \eta \leq 1/L,
$$
preserves the rates of ch. 2 ($O(1/k)$, linear under strong convexity).

::: proof
**Projection lemma.** For every $y \in \mathcal{C}$,
$$
\langle x - \Pi_\mathcal{C}(x),\, y - \Pi_\mathcal{C}(x)\rangle \leq 0 :
$$
otherwise the point
$$
\Pi_\mathcal{C}(x) + \varepsilon(y - \Pi_\mathcal{C}(x)) \in \mathcal{C}
$$
(by convexity) would be closer to $x$ for small $\varepsilon > 0$ — contradicting the definition of the projection.

With $p_k = x_k - \eta\nabla f(x_k)$ and $x_{k+1} = \Pi_\mathcal{C}(p_k)$, the same computation as in theorem 2.2 applies, the extra cross term being precisely controlled by the lemma (taken at $y = x^\star$). [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 8.4 — Penalty and multiplier on the simplest constrained problem]{.tag} Minimize $\tfrac12 x^2$ subject to $x \geq 1$, i.e. $g(x) = 1 - x \leq 0$; the solution is $x^\star = 1$.

*Penalty.* Minimizing $\tfrac12 x^2 + \tfrac{\rho}{2}(1 - x)_+^2$ gives
$$
x_\rho = \frac{\rho}{1+\rho} :
$$
the constraint is violated by $\frac{1}{1+\rho}$, which vanishes only as $\rho \to \infty$ — and the curvature $1 + \rho$ of the penalized function grows at the same time, so the problem becomes ill-conditioned.

*Multiplier (Uzawa).* The Lagrangian $\tfrac12 x^2 + \lambda(1 - x)$ is minimized at $x(\lambda) = \lambda$, so the dual function is $d(\lambda) = \lambda - \tfrac12\lambda^2$, maximized at
$$
\lambda^\star = 1, \qquad d(\lambda^\star) = \tfrac12 = f(x^\star) :
$$
no duality gap, as theorem 0.2 predicts. The Uzawa update
$$
\lambda_{k+1} = [\lambda_k + \rho\,(1 - x(\lambda_k))]_+ = [(1-\rho)\lambda_k + \rho]_+
$$
converges to $\lambda^\star = 1$ for any $0 < \rho < 2$, the error being multiplied by $|1 - \rho|$ at each step; at the limit the constraint holds *exactly*.

The multiplier $\lambda^\star = 1$ is also the price of the constraint: tightening it to $x \geq 1 + \delta$ raises the optimal value by about $\lambda^\star\delta = \delta$.
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.5 — SVM: the constraint that becomes a penalty, that becomes a dual]{.tag} Hard-margin SVM (see the Machine Learning module, ch. 3): $\min \tfrac12\|w\|^2$ subject to $y_i w^\top x_i \geq 1$.

1.  The Wolfe dual is
    $$
    \max_\alpha -\tfrac12\|X^\top(\alpha\odot y)\|^2 + \mathbf{1}^\top\alpha \quad \text{subject to} \quad \alpha \geq 0 ,
    $$
    whose feasible set is the non-negative orthant. Its projection clips the negative entries to $0$, so projected descent (theorem 8.3) applies directly. With a bias term $b$ in the margins, the dual gains the constraint $\alpha^\top y = 0$; the soft-margin SVM adds $\alpha_i \leq C$, which makes the feasible set a box.
2.  The regularized primal (hinge):
    $$
    \min \tfrac1n\sum \max(0, 1 - y_i w^\top x_i) + \lambda\|w\|^2
    $$
    is a special case of the $f + g$ form of ch. 4 — this time with a non-smooth $f$, solved by the subgradient method (theorem 4.6) or through its dual.

Three chapters of the module, a single problem.
:::

::: note
[Beyond the empirical optimum: "PAC" constrained learning]{.tag} Satisfying the constraints *on average over the training set* does not guarantee they will hold *in test*. This is the question addressed by L. Chamon (ch. 11): do generalization guarantees exist for learning under requirements? Positive answer (in the PAC framework, under conditions); and the empirical dual approaches the population dual well (empirical duality gap zero under good assumptions). Until ch. 11, remember: duality is not a computational artifact — it is what makes requirements *learnable*.
:::

### Minimax optimization and saddle-point methods

The Lagrangian of definition 8.1 turns a constrained problem into a game: the learner minimizes over $\theta$ while the multiplier maximizes over $\lambda \geq 0$. The same min–max structure appears elsewhere in AI: generative adversarial networks ($\min$ over the generator, $\max$ over the discriminator) and adversarial training:
$$
\min_\theta \mathbb{E}\max_{\|\delta\| \leq \epsilon}\ell(h_\theta(x + \delta), y).
$$
This section studies the algorithms for such problems and shows that they need more care than plain gradient descent.

::: def
[Definition 8.6 — Saddle point, gradient descent–ascent]{.tag} For $\mathcal{L}(x, y)$, convex in $x$ and concave in $y$, a **saddle point** $(x^\star, y^\star)$ satisfies
$$
\mathcal{L}(x^\star, y) \leq \mathcal{L}(x^\star, y^\star) \leq \mathcal{L}(x, y^\star) \quad \text{for all } x, y :
$$
no player gains by moving alone. On compact convex sets, the minimax theorem (von Neumann, Sion) guarantees $\min_x\max_y \mathcal{L} = \max_y\min_x \mathcal{L}$, the game version of strong duality (theorem 0.2).

**Simultaneous gradient descent–ascent** (GDA) updates
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\nabla_x\mathcal{L}(x_k, y_k), \qquad y_{k+1} = y_k + \eta\nabla_y\mathcal{L}(x_k, y_k),
$$
with a projection when $y$ is constrained (for multipliers, $y \geq 0$). The primal-dual methods of proposition 8.2 are of this type, with the primal step replaced by one gradient step.
:::

::: ex
[Example 8.7 — The bilinear game: GDA spirals out, extragradient converges]{.tag} Take $\mathcal{L}(x, y) = xy$ on $\mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}$; its unique saddle point is $(0, 0)$.

**GDA** gives $x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta y_k$ and $y_{k+1} = y_k + \eta x_k$, so
$$
x_{k+1}^2 + y_{k+1}^2 = (1 + \eta^2)(x_k^2 + y_k^2) :
$$
for *every* step size the iterates turn around the saddle point and move away from it.

The **extragradient** method first takes a trial step, $\tilde x = x_k - \eta y_k$ and $\tilde y = y_k + \eta x_k$, then updates from the original point with the gradient evaluated at the trial point:
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\tilde y = (1 - \eta^2)x_k - \eta y_k, \qquad y_{k+1} = y_k + \eta\tilde x = \eta x_k + (1 - \eta^2)y_k.
$$
Now
$$
x_{k+1}^2 + y_{k+1}^2 = \big((1 - \eta^2)^2 + \eta^2\big)(x_k^2 + y_k^2) = (1 - \eta^2 + \eta^4)(x_k^2 + y_k^2),
$$
a factor strictly below $1$ for $0 < \eta < 1$: the iterates converge to the saddle point. The trial step anticipates the rotation that GDA undergoes.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 8.8 — What is known about saddle-point methods (statements)]{.tag}

1.  For $\mathcal{L}$ convex-concave and $G$-Lipschitz on compact convex sets of diameter $D$, GDA with the step $\eta \propto D/(G\sqrt{K})$ and **averaged** iterates reaches a duality gap
    $$
    \max_y\mathcal{L}(\bar x_K, y) - \min_x\mathcal{L}(x, \bar y_K) = O(DG/\sqrt{K})
    $$
    — the subgradient rate of theorem 4.6, the averaging being necessary (example 8.7 shows that the last iterate can diverge).
2.  If the gradient of $\mathcal{L}$ is moreover $L$-Lipschitz, extragradient (the mirror-prox method of Nemirovski, 2004) with step $1/L$ reaches $O(LD^2/K)$ for the averaged iterates.
3.  Without convexity-concavity, as in GANs, there is no general guarantee: GDA can cycle or diverge, which is one reason why GAN training is notoriously unstable.
:::

## 9. Hyperparameter optimization {#ch9}

This chapter optimizes the quantities that the previous chapters took as given. The step $\eta$, the penalty $\lambda$, the batch size, the learning rate schedule: so many hyperparameters that the module has so far treated as given. Yet experience shows they are often worth more performance points than the choice of algorithm itself. The task is to optimize *the optimizer* itself.

::: def
[Definition 9.1 — The problem (and why it is hard)]{.tag}
$$
\max_{h \in \mathcal{H}}\; v(h), \qquad v(h) = \text{validation score of a model trained with } h,
$$
an *expensive* function (each evaluation = one training run), *noisy*, *non-convex*, with no gradient available. Typically 5 to 50 dimensions, a budget of 10 to 1,000 evaluations. This is the territory of Bayesian *derivative-free* optimization.
:::

:::: prop
[Proposition 9.2 — Grid vs random (Bergstra–Bengio, argument)]{.tag} With a budget of $B$ trials and $p$ "important" hyperparameters out of $d$: the grid explores $B^{1/d}$ values per dimension, random sampling explores $B$ per dimension (but only once per draw).

If only $p \ll d$ parameters really matter, random search hits a good combination on those $p$ with much higher probability: in a grid, every "good" cell on the $p$ useful axes is duplicated across the $d-p$ useless ones — a wasted budget.

::: proof
Model: a cell is "good" if its coordinates on the $p$ useful axes are good, probability $q^p$ per random draw ($q$ = fraction of good values per axis) — after $B$ draws, the probability of touching none:
$$
(1-q^p)^B .
$$
In a regular grid of $m = B^{1/d}$ values per axis: the number of combinations explored on the useful axes is
$$
m^p = B^{p/d} \ll B .
$$
As soon as $p < d$, $B^{p/d} < B$: the grid visits fewer useful regions at equal budget. [∎]{.qed}
:::
::::

::: ex
[Example 9.3 — The numbers for 64 trials]{.tag} Two hyperparameters, of which only the learning rate matters, and good values occupying $5\%$ of its range ($q = 0.05$). 

-   **Grid.** A grid of $8 \times 8 = 64$ trials tests only $8$ distinct learning rates; even with a random offset, a grid of $8$ equally spaced points hits an interval of length $0.05$ with probability $8 \times 0.05 = 0.4$, so it misses the good region with probability $0.6$.
-   **Random.** Sixty-four random trials test $64$ distinct learning rates and miss with probability $0.95^{64} \approx 0.04$.

Same budget, fifteen times fewer failures.
:::

::: def
[Definition 9.4 — Bayesian optimization (GP-EI)]{.tag}

1.  Model: $v \sim \mathrm{GP}(0, k)$ over $\mathcal{H}$; after $k$ evaluations, Gaussian predictions $(\mu_k(h), \sigma_k(h))$ at every point.
2.  *Expected improvement* acquisition: with $v_k^\star = \max_j v(h_j)$,
    $$
    \mathrm{EI}_k(h) = \mathbb{E}\big[(v(h) - v_k^\star)_+\big] = (\mu_k(h) - v_k^\star)\,\Phi(z_k(h)) + \sigma_k(h)\,\varphi(z_k(h)), \quad z_k = \frac{\mu_k - v_k^\star}{\sigma_k}.
    $$
3.  Loop: evaluate $h_{k+1} = \arg\max_h \mathrm{EI}_k(h)$, update the GP.

The closed-form formula shows the exploitation/exploration mechanics: $\mathrm{EI}$ grows when $\mu$ exceeds the record (*exploit*) and when $\sigma$ is large (*explore*).
:::

::: note
[Multi-fidelity: Hyperband, pragmatism]{.tag} When the evaluation has a "quality setting" (epochs, data subsample), launching many configurations cheaply and only pursuing the promising ones often dominates pure GP: this is Successive Halving and Hyperband (Li et al., 2017), ubiquitous in practice (optuna, ray tune). The practitioner's reference trio: random to scout, Hyperband to dig, GP-EI for the 5–10 truly sensitive parameters.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
def train_score(lr, lam, epochs=30):          # proxy: linear reg model
    # ... real training replaced by a rugged function
    peak = 0.92 - 0.4*np.abs(np.log10(lr) + 1.5) - 0.15*np.log10(1+lam)
    return peak + 0.02*np.sin(10*lr) + 0.01*rng.standard_normal()

best_grid = max(train_score(10**e, 10**-l)
                for e in np.linspace(-4, -1, 8) for l in np.linspace(0, 3, 8))
best_rand = max(train_score(10**rng.uniform(-4, -1), 10**-rng.uniform(0, 3))
                for _ in range(64))           # same budget: 64 trials
print("grid:", round(best_grid, 4), "random:", round(best_rand, 4))
# on this type of landscape (few sensitive parameters), random almost always wins
```
:::

## 10. Optimizing the training of networks {#ch10}

This chapter confronts the module with its main application. Almost everything so far assumed convexity, and training a network is not convex. Yet the recipes of deep learning are literally the objects of the previous chapters, transplanted — with adaptations that non-convexity demands.

::: note
[What survives, what breaks]{.tag}

| Module object (convex) | Deep learning transplant | Status |
|---|---|---|
| gradient descent (ch. 2) | backprop + SGD (see Deep Learning, ch. 2–3) | works; no global guarantee |
| momentum/Nesterov (ch. 3) | SGD+momentum 0.9 | empirically: yes, big gains |
| rate $\kappa$, linear convergence (ch. 2–3) | non-convex landscape: plateaus, passes, valleys | replaced by heuristics (warmup, cosine) |
| proximal/ISTA (ch. 4) | weight decay, structured regularization | first-order analogue for $\ell_2$ (AdamW, recall 10.1) |
| SGD: variance (ch. 5) | batch size, grad clipping | strong analogy, partial theory |
| hyperparameters (ch. 9) | learning rate = hyperparameter #1 | identical |
:::

:::: recap
::: recap-title
Recall 10.1 — Adam and AdamW (taught in [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch3), sections 3.3 and 3.6), read with the module's tools
:::

Adam (Kingma–Ba, 2015) accumulates two exponential moments of the stochastic gradient $g_k$:
$$
m_k = \beta_1 m_{k-1} + (1-\beta_1)g_k, \qquad v_k = \beta_2 v_{k-1} + (1-\beta_2)g_k^2,
$$
and updates
$$
x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\, \hat m_k / (\sqrt{\hat v_k} + \varepsilon).
$$

"Module" reading:

-   $m_k$ is heavy-ball momentum (ch. 3), an exponential average of past gradients; the Nesterov variant is NAdam;
-   $1/\sqrt{v_k}$ is a *per-coordinate* step adapted to the observed gradient scale (ch. 5: the noise is damped, not removed);
-   the bias correction $\hat\cdot$ fixes the initialization of the moments at zero.

AdamW (Loshchilov–Hutter, 2019) takes the weight decay out of the gradient: the shrinkage $x \leftarrow (1-\eta\lambda)x$ is applied separately, outside the adaptive scaling. It is an explicit gradient step on $\tfrac{\lambda}{2}\|x\|^2$, which agrees to first order in $\eta\lambda$ with the proximal step $x/(1+\eta\lambda)$ of ch. 4. Inside Adam, the same penalty would be divided by $\sqrt{\hat v_k}$, so the two choices give different trajectories.
::::

::: note
[Learning rate schedule: warmup, cosine, large batch]{.tag} The recipes are those of [Deep Learning](../m1p1-deep-learning/index.html#ch3), section 3.4; what is new here is their reading through chapter 5.

-   **Warmup**: in the first iterations, the moments $v_k$ are poorly estimated and the activations of deep networks poorly calibrated (variance that explodes with depth — see Deep Learning, ch. 1); ramping $\eta$ linearly over 0.5–2% of the budget avoids destructive first steps.
-   **Cosine / step decay**: reducing $\eta$ at the end of training shrinks the $O(\eta\sigma^2)$ neighborhood of theorem 5.2 — exactly the Robbins–Monro logic, in practical form.
-   **Large batch**: with the batch multiplied by $k$, variance $\sigma^2/k$, but fewer steps per epoch; the "linear rule" ($\eta \to k\eta$) fails beyond a threshold; LARS/LAMB (You et al., 2017–2020) normalize the step by the per-layer weight/gradient norm — a heuristic, but the one that trained BERT and the LLMs.
:::

::: prop
[Proposition 10.2 — Why it works anyway (overview)]{.tag} Three shock absorbers explain why non-convexity is not prohibitive:

1.  *overparameterization*: with more parameters than constraints, local minima become rare — all connected and of similar value;
2.  *local PL inequality*: along trajectories, an analogue of the Polyak–Łojasiewicz condition (ch. 2) often holds empirically, which restores local linear convergence "as if";
3.  *SGD noise*: the stationary regime (prop. 5.4) sweeps narrow passes and selects flat minima that generalize better.

None of the three is a general theorem — this is precisely the research frontier of the field. Optional reading: the complexity of training seen from the efficiency side is ch. 8 of [Deep Learning (P2 variant)](../m1p2-deep-learning-p2/index.html#ch8), a sibling option of the same group.
:::

::: note
[The engineer's reflex sheet]{.tag} Diagnosing a diverging training run:

1.  $\eta$ too large — divide by 10 (th. 5.2: the neighborhood grows as $\eta\sigma^2$);
2.  no warmup;
3.  faulty initialization/normalization (see Deep Learning, ch. 1);
4.  exploding gradient — clipping ($g \mapsto \min(1, c/\|g\|)\,g$, a projection of ch. 8 onto a ball).

A "flat" training run: step too small, batch too large, or missing momentum. These reflexes *are* chapters 2, 3 and 5.
:::

### Adaptive methods: AdaGrad, and what Adam changes

Recall 10.1 presented Adam as a recipe. Its theoretical ancestor is AdaGrad, for which a clean guarantee exists, and comparing the two shows what is gained and what is lost when the step adapts to the observed gradients.

:::: def
[Definition 10.3 — AdaGrad (Duchi, Hazan & Singer 2011)]{.tag} With $g_k$ the stochastic gradient at step $k$, accumulate the squared gradients coordinate by coordinate, $G_{k,i} = \sum_{j \leq k} g_{j,i}^2$, and update

::: key
[Key result — the AdaGrad step]{.tag}
$$
x_{k+1,i} = x_{k,i} - \frac{\eta}{\sqrt{G_{k,i}} + \varepsilon}\, g_{k,i}, \qquad i = 1, \dots, d.
$$
:::

Each coordinate receives its own step, large for coordinates whose gradients have been small or rare, small for those whose gradients have been large. RMSProp and Adam replace the sum $G_{k,i}$ by an exponential moving average $v_{k,i}$, which forgets old gradients.
::::

::: thm
[Theorem 10.4 — Regret of AdaGrad (Duchi, Hazan & Singer 2011, admitted)]{.tag} In online convex optimization (convex losses $f_k$ revealed one at a time, iterates kept in a convex set of $\ell_\infty$-diameter $D_\infty$ by projection), diagonal AdaGrad with $\eta = D_\infty/\sqrt{2}$ satisfies
$$
\sum_{k=1}^{T}\big(f_k(x_k) - f_k(x^\star)\big) \;\leq\; \sqrt{2}\, D_\infty \sum_{i=1}^{d}\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{T} g_{k,i}^2\Big)^{1/2}.
$$
Averaging the iterates turns this into a stochastic convex rate $\mathbb{E}f(\bar x_T) - f(x^\star) \leq \text{regret}/T$.

In the worst case, the right-hand side is of order $D_\infty G_\infty\, d\sqrt{T}$, no better than tuned SGD; when most coordinates are rarely active (sparse features, as in text), it is much smaller — and it is obtained *without* knowing the scale of the gradients.
:::

::: ex
[Example 10.5 — Scale-free steps]{.tag} In one dimension, suppose that every gradient equals the same constant $c \neq 0$. AdaGrad's step at iteration $k$ is, in absolute value, whatever $c$,
$$
\eta c/\sqrt{k c^2} = \eta/\sqrt{k} :
$$
multiplying the loss by $100$ changes nothing, whereas plain SGD would need its step divided by $100$. The method recovers by itself the decreasing $1/\sqrt{k}$ schedule of chapter 5.

For a coordinate that is non-zero only in a fraction $p$ of the steps, with gradients of size $c$ when active, $G_{k} \approx p k c^2$ and the effective step on active steps is $\eta/\sqrt{pk}$. Rare features get steps $1/\sqrt{p}$ times larger, which is why AdaGrad was first adopted for sparse linear models in language processing.

The price of forgetting: by replacing the sum with a moving average, Adam can lose this guarantee — Reddi, Kale & Kumar (ICLR 2018) build a simple convex online problem on which Adam does not converge, and propose AMSGrad, which uses the running maximum of $v_k$ in the denominator so that the effective steps never increase.
:::

### Lab: diagnosing a diverging run

The reflex sheet above, tested on a small network. The code below trains a one-hidden-layer tanh network by full-batch gradient descent. It also measures the *sharpness*, the largest eigenvalue of the Hessian, by power iteration on gradient differences, without ever forming the Hessian.

::: ex
[Example 10.6 — Step, sharpness, clipping and warmup]{.tag} The one-dimensional analysis of chapter 2 predicts trouble above
$$
\eta = 2/\text{sharpness},
$$
which here is about $0.74$ at initialization.

```python
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n, d, h = 512, 10, 32                       # one-hidden-layer tanh network
X = rng.normal(size=(n, d))
```
